title: Composition over inheritance: why almost always

videos.script: Most courses teach inheritance first. It is the feature that makes a language feel object oriented. This lesson argues that you should reach for it last, and it shows why with programs rather than slogans. {{title}} First, a shelf that counts what goes on it. The count comes out wrong, and nothing in the counting code is wrong. A line inside the parent class broke it. {{fragile}} Then a count of a different kind. Four things vary in a loan, and one subclass per combination comes to thirty-six classes. Built from parts, the same choices need ten. {{explosion}} After that, the remedy. An object that holds another and forwards to it is immune to the line that broke the shelf. {{delegation}} A loan that holds its fine rule can change the rule while the program runs, for every loan already out on the shelves. {{swap}} Inheritance still has its places, and you will see three of them. Errors, skeletons with holes, and frameworks that ask for it. {{fits}} Python adds a fourth tool, the mixin, which is composition delivered through inheritance, with both of their habits. {{mixins}} And at the end, you take a real hierarchy apart, one step at a time, with the same tests passing at every step. {{refactor}}
